slides.body: Six mistakes to watch for.

items: Reading a large diff top to bottom. Root cause: a patch is ordered by path, not by importance; --stat, --name-status and --diff-filter show where to look first.
Treating "renamed" as a recorded fact. Root cause: Git stores no renames; the letter R is an inference from similarity at or above a threshold, 50% by default.
Moving a file and rewriting it in the same commit. Root cause: similarity falls below the threshold, and every tool that relies on rename detection then sees a deletion and an addition.
Assuming -w hides everything a formatter did. Root cause: -w ignores whitespace only; quote changes and line re-wrapping are content.
Comparing "lines changed" from two tools. Root cause: the count is a property of the diff algorithm, not of the commit.
Running git diff --check after git add -A and seeing a clean result. Root cause: the unstaged diff is empty; --cached inspects what will be committed.

beats.text: Diffs, renames, "who wrote this line" and "which commit broke it" are not recorded anywhere. Git computes them when you ask, with heuristics that have thresholds and blind spots. An investigator has to know which answers are facts read from objects and which are inferences.
beats.tele: Diffs, renames, "who wrote this line" and "which commit broke it" are not recorded anywhere. Git computes them when you ask, with heuristics that have thresholds and blind spots. An investigator has to know which answers are facts read from objects and which are inferences.

beats.text: Today that principle is applied to the most basic tool, the diff. Four things. Summaries and filters, which answer "what changed" before "how". Renames and copies, which are computed and can be missed. Whitespace and word-level views, which read through reformatting. And diff algorithms, which decide how one and the same change is displayed. At the end comes --check, a small guard that belongs before every commit.

beats.text: Renames and copies. In one sentence: a commit does not say "this file was renamed". git diff notices that a path disappeared, another appeared, and their contents are similar enough. On screen, one stored file: run_eval.py, with the ID of its content, its blob ID.

beats.text: Precisely. Rename detection is a pass over the list of changed paths. A deleted path and an added path with the same blob ID are an exact rename. For the remaining pairs Git computes a similarity index, and a pair at or above the threshold becomes a rename. On screen the two blob IDs differ, so this pair needs the similarity index.
beats.tele: Precisely. Rename detection is a pass over the list of changed paths. A deleted path and an added path with the same blob ID are an exact rename. For the remaining pairs Git computes a similarity index, and a pair at or above the threshold becomes a rename. On screen the two blob IDs differ, so this pair needs the similarity index.

beats.text: The threshold is 50 percent by default. -M<n> changes it, and --no-renames switches the pass off. For the porcelain commands the pass is on by default. -C also looks for copies, with the sources limited to files that the same commit modified. --find-copies-harder, or -C given twice, considers every file of the older tree and costs accordingly.
beats.tele: The threshold is 50 percent by default. `-M<n>` changes it, and `--no-renames` switches the pass off. For the porcelain commands the pass is on by default. `-C` also looks for copies, with the sources limited to files that the same commit modified. `--find-copies-harder`, or `-C` given twice, considers every file of the older tree and costs accordingly.

beats.text: The limit: similarity is a heuristic over content. Rename a file and rewrite half of it in the same commit, and the link is gone. Everything that relies on rename detection inherits this limit: git log --follow, git blame, and the rename handling of git merge, which you met in the merge module as a modify/delete conflict that nobody intended.

beats.text: Noise. Two kinds of change bury the lines you are looking for: whitespace, and small edits inside long lines. -w treats lines that differ only in whitespace as equal. --word-diff compares words and marks them in place.

beats.text: Algorithms. In one sentence: for two given files there are many correct diffs, and the algorithm decides which one you read.
beats.tele: Algorithms. In one sentence: for two given files there are many correct diffs, and the algorithm decides which one you read.

beats.text: Git has four. myers, the default, which the manual calls "the basic greedy diff algorithm". minimal, which spends extra time to produce the smallest diff. patience. And histogram, which "extends the patience algorithm to support low-occurrence common elements". The last two anchor on lines that occur rarely, which tends to keep moved blocks together. Choose with --diff-algorithm=<name> and make the choice permanent with diff.algorithm.

And `histogram`, which "extends the patience algorithm to support low-occurrence common elements". The last two anchor on lines that occur rarely, which tends to keep moved blocks together. Choose with `--diff-algorithm=<name>` and make the choice permanent with `diff.algorithm`.

beats.text: --check is not about reading diffs at all. It inspects the lines a diff adds and reports whitespace errors and leftover conflict markers, with an exit status a script can test.

beats.text: Inferences: "this file was renamed". "These six lines were edited" as opposed to "this block moved". "42 lines changed". Each of those depends on a threshold or an algorithm, and a different setting gives a different, equally valid answer.

beats.text: Think of a map drawn from two aerial photographs taken a year apart. The photographs are facts. "This building was moved" is the cartographer's inference from "a building vanished here, a similar one appeared there". Usually right. Wrong when the building was also half rebuilt.

beats.text: Ten files, 104 insertions, 31 deletions. One line per file, with a histogram. You now know where the bulk is before you have read a single changed line.
beats.tele: Ten files, 104 insertions, 31 deletions. One line per file, with a histogram. You now know where the bulk is before you have read a single changed line.

beats.text: --name-status: A for added, M for modified, and one D: scorekit/bleu.py was deleted between v0.1.0 and main.
beats.tele: `--name-status`: `A` for added, `M` for modified, and one `D`: `scorekit/bleu.py` was deleted between `v0.1.0` and `main`.

beats.text: --numstat gives the form for scripts: added, removed, path.
beats.tele: `--numstat` gives the form for scripts: added, removed, path.

beats.text: --diff-filter=A lists only additions, =D only deletions, and lowercase ad excludes both and leaves the modifications. --diff-filter=D with git log is the standard way to find when a file was deleted. A later video uses it.
beats.tele: `--diff-filter=A` lists only additions, `=D` only deletions, and lowercase `ad` excludes both and leaves the modifications. `--diff-filter=D` with `git log` is the standard way to find when a file was deleted. A later video uses it.

beats.text: A pathspec, a pattern that limits a command to some paths, after the double dash narrows any of these, including the exclusion form.
beats.tele: A pathspec, a pattern that limits a command to some paths, after the double dash narrows any of these, including the exclusion form.

beats.text: Part 2: renames are computed. labs/run ch14a/diff-renames. Between commit d369eac and v0.1.0 the sources moved into a package, one module was renamed a second time, and two files were edited on the way.
beats.tele: Part 2: renames are computed. `labs/run ch14a/diff-renames`. Between commit `d369eac` and `v0.1.0` the sources moved into a package, one module was renamed a second time, and two files were edited on the way.

beats.text: R100 is an exact rename: two commits moved scorer.py twice and never changed it, and the diff of the endpoints sees one rename. R090 and R082 are renames with edits. Predict the same comparison with --no-renames. Say it out loud. I'll wait.
beats.tele: `R100` is an exact rename: two commits moved `scorer.py` twice and never changed it, and the diff of the endpoints sees one rename. `R090` and `R082` are renames with edits. Predict the same comparison with `--no-renames`. Say it out loud. I'll wait.

beats.text: A list of unrelated deletions and additions. Same two trees, same facts, different inference. The threshold decides.
beats.tele: A list of unrelated deletions and additions. Same two trees, same facts, different inference. The threshold decides.

beats.text: At 90 percent the runner, whose similarity is 82 percent, is no longer a rename: it's a D and an A.
beats.tele: At 90 percent the runner, whose similarity is 82 percent, is no longer a rename: it's a `D` and an `A`.

beats.text: In a patch, a detected rename is printed as extended header lines, "similarity index 82%", "rename from", "rename to", and only the changed lines follow.
beats.tele: In a patch, a detected rename is printed as extended header lines, "similarity index 82%", "rename from", "rename to", and only the changed lines follow.

beats.text: And --stat shows a rename in one line, with the old and the new name.
beats.tele: And `--stat` shows a rename in one line, with the old and the new name.

beats.text: Copies need the harder search when the source file was not modified by the same commit. Here Asha seeded the nightly data set from the smoke set.
beats.tele: Copies need the harder search when the source file was not modified by the same commit. Here Asha seeded the nightly data set from the smoke set.

beats.text: -C alone finds nothing, because data/smoke.jsonl itself did not change in that commit. --find-copies-harder finds the copy with a similarity of 71 percent and reduces fourteen added lines to the four that are new.
beats.tele: `-C` alone finds nothing, because `data/smoke.jsonl` itself did not change in that commit. `--find-copies-harder` finds the copy with a similarity of 71 percent and reduces fourteen added lines to the four that are new.

beats.text: Now the limit. A file renamed and half rewritten in one step. Predict what git status shows. I'll wait.
beats.tele: Now the limit. A file renamed and half rewritten in one step. Predict what `git status` shows. I'll wait.

beats.text: A deletion and an addition, because status uses the default threshold and this pair is 43 percent similar. A lower threshold still finds it, but nobody reading the log later will think to pass -M40%. Moving and tidying in one commit feels natural. Almost everyone does it once.
beats.tele: A deletion and an addition, because status uses the default threshold and this pair is 43 percent similar. A lower threshold still finds it, but nobody reading the log later will think to pass `-M40%`. Moving and tidying in one commit feels natural. Almost everyone does it once.

beats.text: Part 3: reading through noise. labs/run ch14a/diff-words-whitespace. Commit 9c8df98 ran a formatter over the sources. That's the commit from the opening.
beats.tele: Part 3: reading through noise. `labs/run ch14a/diff-words-whitespace`. Commit `9c8df98` ran a formatter over the sources. That's the commit from the opening.

beats.text: Without -w: five files, 40 lines. With -w: three files, 11 lines.
beats.tele: Without `-w`: five files, 40 lines. With `-w`: three files, 11 lines.

beats.text: The 40 lines from the opening have shrunk. Two files drop out entirely: their only change was the indentation. What are the eleven lines that remain?
beats.tele: The 40 lines from the opening have shrunk. Two files drop out entirely: their only change was the indentation. What are the eleven lines that remain?

beats.text: The formatter also replaced single quotes with double quotes. That is not whitespace, so -w cannot hide it.
beats.tele: The formatter also replaced single quotes with double quotes. That is not whitespace, so `-w` cannot hide it.

beats.text: Remember this split: it returns in the blame videos, where git blame -w sees through the indentation and needs a different option for the quotes.
beats.tele: Remember this split: it returns in the blame videos, where `git blame -w` sees through the indentation and needs a different option for the quotes.

beats.text: For prose, configuration strings and long lines, a line-based diff says "this line changed" and leaves the comparison to your eyes.
beats.tele: For prose, configuration strings and long lines, a line-based diff says "this line changed" and leaves the comparison to your eyes.

beats.text: Two long lines removed, two long lines added. Try it now. Thirty seconds: find the difference in the last pair, without help.
beats.tele: Two long lines removed, two long lines added. Try it now. Thirty seconds: find the difference in the last pair, without help.

beats.text: --word-diff marks removed text in square brackets with minus signs and added text in braces with plus signs. "token" became "token-level". And in the last line, three words were removed: "lowercases the text,". In the line-based diff that removal was hard to see. Here it's marked.
beats.tele: `--word-diff` marks removed text in square brackets with minus signs and added text in braces with plus signs. "token" became "token-level". And in the last line, three words were removed: "lowercases the text,". In the line-based diff that removal was hard to see. Here it's marked.

beats.text: The output of --word-diff is for reading, not for git apply.
beats.tele: The output of `--word-diff` is for reading, not for `git apply`.

beats.text: Part 4: algorithms. labs/run ch14a/diff-algorithms. One file, two similar functions, and an edit that swaps them. Nothing else changed.
beats.tele: Part 4: algorithms. `labs/run ch14a/diff-algorithms`. One file, two similar functions, and an edit that swaps them. Nothing else changed.

beats.text: Myers found the shortest edit: six lines out, six lines in. It is correct, and it tells a false story, that someone edited both functions line by line.
beats.tele: Myers found the shortest edit: six lines out, six lines in. It is correct, and it tells a false story, that someone edited both functions line by line.

beats.text: Histogram tells what happened: one function removed from the top and added at the bottom, unchanged.
beats.tele: Histogram tells what happened: one function removed from the top and added at the bottom, unchanged.

beats.text: And the line counts differ: 6 and 6 under Myers, 7 and 7 under histogram and patience. Same two files.
beats.tele: And the line counts differ: 6 and 6 under Myers, 7 and 7 under histogram and patience. Same two files.

beats.text: diff.algorithm makes the choice permanent.
beats.tele: `diff.algorithm` makes the choice permanent.

beats.text: Part 5: --check. labs/run ch14a/diff-check. A line with two trailing spaces in config.py, a forgotten conflict marker in docs/metrics.md.
beats.tele: Part 5: `--check`. `labs/run ch14a/diff-check`. A line with two trailing spaces in `config.py`, a forgotten conflict marker in `docs/metrics.md`.

beats.text: Both reported, with file and line, and exit status 2. Now you run git add -A, which stages everything, and check again. Quick quiz, two options. Option one: the same two reports. Option two: nothing at all. Say it out loud.
beats.tele: Both reported, with file and line, and exit status 2. Now you run `git add -A`, which stages everything, and check again. Quick quiz, two options. Option one: the same two reports. Option two: nothing at all. Say it out loud.

beats.text: Option two. After git add -A the unstaged diff is empty, so the first command finds nothing: exit status 0.
beats.tele: Option two. After `git add -A` the unstaged diff is empty, so the first command finds nothing: exit status 0.

beats.text: git diff --cached --check inspects what the next commit would record. As with every form of git diff, which changes are inspected depends on the operands.
beats.tele: `git diff --cached --check` inspects what the next commit would record. As with every form of `git diff`, which changes are inspected depends on the operands.

beats.text: With two commits as operands it's the form for continuous integration, the automated checks on each change.
beats.tele: With two commits as operands it's the form for continuous integration, the automated checks on each change.

beats.text: Six mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Six mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Reading a large diff top to bottom. Root cause: a patch is ordered by path, not by importance; --stat, --name-status and --diff-filter show where to look first.
beats.tele: Reading a large diff top to bottom. Root cause: a patch is ordered by path, not by importance; `--stat`, `--name-status` and `--diff-filter` show where to look first.

beats.text: Treating "renamed" as a recorded fact. Root cause: Git stores no renames; the letter R is an inference from similarity at or above a threshold, 50% by default.
beats.tele: Treating "renamed" as a recorded fact. Root cause: Git stores no renames; the letter `R` is an inference from similarity at or above a threshold, 50% by default.

beats.text: Moving a file and rewriting it in the same commit. Root cause: similarity falls below the threshold, and every tool that relies on rename detection then sees a deletion and an addition.
beats.tele: Moving a file and rewriting it in the same commit. Root cause: similarity falls below the threshold, and every tool that relies on rename detection then sees a deletion and an addition.

beats.text: Assuming -w hides everything a formatter did. Root cause: -w ignores whitespace only; quote changes and line re-wrapping are content.
beats.tele: Assuming `-w` hides everything a formatter did. Root cause: `-w` ignores whitespace only; quote changes and line re-wrapping are content.

beats.text: Comparing "lines changed" from two tools. Root cause: the count is a property of the diff algorithm, not of the commit.
beats.tele: Comparing "lines changed" from two tools. Root cause: the count is a property of the diff algorithm, not of the commit.

beats.text: Running git diff --check after git add -A and seeing a clean result. Root cause: the unstaged diff is empty; --cached inspects what will be committed.
beats.tele: Running `git diff --check` after `git add -A` and seeing a clean result. Root cause: the unstaged diff is empty; `--cached` inspects what will be committed.

beats.text: Now, out of the lab. Three rules that a model-evaluation team can take from this part of the textbook.
beats.tele: Now, out of the lab. Three rules that a model-evaluation team can take from this part of the textbook.

beats.text: Rename in one commit, edit in the next. A commit that only moves files shows R100 everywhere, reviews in seconds, and keeps every history tool working. The textbook adds two limits that matter on large changes: the inexact comparison is quadratic in the number of unpaired files and is skipped above diff.renameLimit candidates, 1000 by default according to the local manual, so a directory move with hundreds of edited files can degrade to deletions and additions.
beats.tele: Rename in one commit, edit in the next. A commit that only moves files shows `R100` everywhere, reviews in seconds, and keeps every history tool working. The textbook adds two limits that matter on large changes: the inexact comparison is quadratic in the number of unpaired files and is skipped above `diff.renameLimit` candidates, 1000 by default according to the local manual, so a directory move with hundreds of edited files can degrade to deletions and additions.

beats.text: Set diff.algorithm=histogram. Many teams do, and the ort merge strategy already uses histogram internally. Remember the three consequences the textbook lists. "Lines changed" is a property of the algorithm. A patch is still valid under any algorithm, because all of them transform the same old file into the same new file. And the algorithm changes what git blame and git log -L attribute, since both run diffs internally.
beats.tele: Set `diff.algorithm=histogram`. Many teams do, and the `ort` merge strategy already uses histogram internally. Remember the three consequences the textbook lists. "Lines changed" is a property of the algorithm. A patch is still valid under any algorithm, because all of them transform the same old file into the same new file. And the algorithm changes what `git blame` and `git log -L` attribute, since both run diffs internally.

beats.text: And git diff --cached --check in a pre-commit hook, a script Git runs before each commit, with the two-commit form in CI. It's the same check that the merge module recommended before concluding a merge: leftover conflict markers are caught before they become a syntax error on main.
beats.tele: And `git diff --cached --check` in a pre-commit hook, a script Git runs before each commit, with the two-commit form in CI. It's the same check that the merge module recommended before concluding a merge: leftover conflict markers are caught before they become a syntax error on `main`.

beats.text: Q399: "Git stores no renames. Name three commands whose output depends on rename detection, and describe a commit that defeats it."
beats.tele: Q399: "Git stores no renames. Name three commands whose output depends on rename detection, and describe a commit that defeats it."

beats.text: Answer out loud first. A strong answer starts by saying what Git does store and how a rename is inferred from it, with the threshold. It names three commands from different areas, so that the examiner sees you know the heuristic is shared: one that compares, one that follows history, one that integrates. The commit that defeats it should be described precisely enough that someone could make it, with a number for the similarity. Finish with the practice that avoids the problem.

beats.text: Git stores no renames. R and C are computed from similarity with a 50 percent default threshold, so a move plus a rewrite in one commit appears as a deletion and an addition.
beats.tele: Git stores no renames. `R` and `C` are computed from similarity with a 50 percent default threshold, so a move plus a rewrite in one commit appears as a deletion and an addition.

beats.text: -w removes whitespace-only changes, and --word-diff shows what changed inside a line. The same change can be displayed differently by myers and histogram, with different line counts, and both are correct. git diff --cached --check finds whitespace errors and leftover conflict markers in what I am about to commit.
